pm_summary: Macro is the whole batch. Open the Journal episode first — the Fed hiked for the first time in three years under Warsh, against White House messaging, with the chain running from Hormuz through oil. Then BofA on the BOJ for the FX-versus-rates dislocation. BofA's eleven minutes on derivative income is the one closest to your shelf. On AI, take Brown on agent swarms and Ghodsi on enterprise reality; the safety-discourse episodes are largely one story told three times.

items.title: The Fed hiked for the first time in three years; Warsh reframes the mandate and the causal chain runs through Hormuz
items.why: Listen first. Twenty-one minutes for the regime change itself, from the WSJ reporter who was in the room: 1) the Fed raised rather than cut, against explicit White House messaging that inflation is contained, 2) the new chair is framing it as fixing a five-year error, which is a reaction-function statement, not a data-point statement, and 3) the causal chain is traced to a supply shock, which tells you what would have to reverse.
key_points: The Fed raised rates for the first time in three years — 'we had been cutting, we stopped cutting, that was a change, and now we're actually going to raise'.

Chair is Kevin Warsh, appointed by Trump in January and in post since May. The market read at appointment was that he opens the door to looser policy; he has delivered the opposite (-ve for the political-capture thesis).
The hike lands while the White House is publicly saying inflation is under control and high prices will fall back soon. The Fed is explicitly disagreeing.
Causal chain as told: the bombing campaign in Iran, then Iran closing the Strait of Hormuz, then the oil spike feeding through to business and consumer costs. A supply shock, not demand.

Warsh's framing — 'that's an important message we've missed for five years, and we're going to fix that' — was received in the room as a bold statement. Read it as a reaction function, not a forecast.
Transmission called out explicitly: mortgages, car loans, credit card balances all reprice higher, alongside the bond market turmoil already in train.
Press conference was run one question, no follow-ups — itself a signal on how much the new chair intends to be interrogated.
items.read_across: This is a reaction-function change, not a data print. Everything positioned for a cutting cycle — duration, rate-sensitive equity, carry — is on the wrong side of it. The Hormuz dependency is the thing to monitor for a reversal.

items.title: BofA on the BOJ: hike delivered, October priced out to 18%, December still base case — and the FX move outran the rates move
items.why: Listen. Recorded Friday 18 Sep, the day of the BOJ decision, with the G10 desk on the call. Twenty minutes for the full sell-side read on a live decision: what was priced, what got repriced, and the one cross-asset dislocation worth trading.
key_points: BOJ raised the policy rate 25bp to 1.25%, as expected, but with two dissents from dovish board members Noda and Sato — both appointed under the current administration, which has fed speculation about political pressure on the BOJ from PM Takaichi.

Post-statement, markets gave back October hike expectations — implied probability down to around 18% — and the 2s30s JGB curve twist-steepened. BofA remains comfortable with a further 25bp at the December meeting as base case.

Governor's press conference was read as balanced, not dovish. BofA's prior was that a 50bp move or back-to-back hikes was never a strong possibility absent an information shock or a behind-the-curve scare of the 2022-23 Fed/ECB type.
The dislocation: 'the FX reaction was much bigger than the rates move implied' against a balanced press conference — i.e. FX is pricing something the rates market is not.

Balance sheet is the longer-dated point. Climate-linked fund-supplying operations were revised so the loan rate is the average policy rate over the life of the loan rather than the rate at extension — no near-term market impact, but it lays the groundwork for tapering liquidity provision.
BofA expects the BOJ balance sheet to shrink at one of the fastest paces among major central banks, via ongoing QT plus the run-off of lending-stimulus facilities.
Net JGB supply relative to nominal GDP is expected to decline in 2027 vs 2026, largely on lower redemptions of BOJ-held JGBs (+ve for JGBs on a supply basis).
items.read_across: The FX-vs-rates divergence is the actionable piece. On the JGB side, supply/GDP falling in 2027 cuts against the consensus supply-indigestion story — relevant if you carry JPY or JGB exposure.

items.title: BofA sizes the derivative-income complex: US$1tn of retail structured issuance, and income ETFs growing 5x the ETF average
items.why: Listen — this is the closest episode of the batch to your own product shelf, and it is eleven minutes. It sizes the structured-income market properly and asks the right question: why is retail reaching for derivative income when traditional yields are back and, after this week's Fed, staying higher. Transcript is incomplete, so treat the framing as solid and the tail figures as indicative.
key_points: US$1tn of retail structured products issued globally last year, 70% equity-linked. Roughly a third of that equity issuance is income-oriented.
Income-oriented issuance has tripled in five years to over US$320bn per annum.
Derivative ETFs have amassed over US$550bn globally, with inflows tripling to US$8bn year-to-date — the highest in at least a decade.
Within derivative ETFs, income-focused strategies — covered calls, put-write and now auto-callables — have grown five times faster than ETFs overall. Auto-call ETFs alone gathered c.US$5bn in a year.
North America specifically: income style is now half of all equity-linked structured issuance.

The demographic argument, with BofA Institute data: 55% of US adults say generating or supplementing regular income is a purpose of investing, led by younger millennials; Gen Z is more than twice as interested in learning about options. Income is no longer a retiree style (+ve for structural demand).
Framed explicitly around the word 'outcome' — predetermined payoffs linked to an index or security — which is the right frame for where auto-callables sit.
items.read_across: Auto-callables are called the workhorse of structured income and are now arriving in ETF wrappers. If you distribute FCN-type product, the ETF wrapper is the competing access point, and the demographic data reframes who the end buyer is.

items.title: OpenAI's Brown on agent swarms: 10,000 agents, 130bn tokens and 88 hours to close a Millennium Prize problem
items.why: Listen. The best available primary account of what parallel test-time compute actually consumes, from the person who built the reasoning models: 1) the resource figures are stated, not estimated, 2) he is explicit about where parallelism stops working, and 3) it is the cleanest read-through to inference demand in the batch.
key_points: OpenAI announced solving one of the Millennium Prize Problems with a system of 10,000 agents consuming 130bn tokens over 88 hours.
Scale in human terms: 130bn tokens is roughly a single human thinking full-time, back to back, for 4,000 years.

The mechanism: reasoning performance scales cleanly with test-time compute, but serial scaling hits a latency wall. Multi-agent is parallel test-time scaling — less efficient per token because no single agent holds all context, but effective.
He is explicit about the limit: 10,000 agents on a novel would not help, the same way 10,000 people writing one novel would not. The gains are task-shaped, not general.

The science is underdone because it is expensive — they have not run single-agent Navier-Stokes, so the speed-up multiple is unknown. Methodical work at 64/128/256 agents is what is needed (-ve for anyone extrapolating from the headline).
items.read_across: If frontier results now require 130bn tokens per problem, inference demand is being driven by agent count, not model size. That is a different capex and power profile than the training-scaling story most compute models still assume.

items.title: Databricks' Ghodsi: enterprise AI is blocked on context not intelligence, cyber is the live risk, and one company at scale moved off frontier models to GLM
items.why: Listen. The operator counterweight to a week of safety discourse, from someone selling into enterprises at scale: 1) a concrete diagnosis of why adoption stalls, 2) a first instance of a scaled company leaving the frontier labs for an open model, and 3) the tragedy-of-the-commons objection to pacing, stated plainly by someone who would have to comply.
key_points: Core diagnosis: 'AI may already be smart enough for the enterprise. The problem is that it doesn't understand your company.' The blocker is organisational context, not model capability (-ve for the pure model-scaling thesis on enterprise revenue).
On pacing the frontier, the commons objection in his own words: 'If you want to go slower, why don't you go slower? I'm competing. I want to win.'
He puts existential risk close to zero today and argues the public probability-of-doom broadcasting causes real harm to people who miss the nuance.

Where he says the risk is real now: cybersecurity. Agents make attacks faster than human security teams can respond, so defence has to be automated — and 'most organizations are actually not close to doing that'.

Stated as a first: 'for the first time ever, a company at scale last week said that they're moving from the frontier models to GLM.' Treated as an open question whether it is a trend or an anecdote (-ve for frontier-lab pricing power if it generalises).
Internal practice at Databricks: built an organisational ontology, actively manages token costs, and routes different models to different jobs rather than defaulting to the best model.
Notes the inconsistency he sees in the discourse — warning humanity will die while discussing IPO allocations, a point he attributes to Elon.
items.read_across: Model routing plus token-cost management at a large buyer is a margin headwind for frontier API pricing. The GLM migration is worth tracking as a leading indicator of open-weight substitution in enterprise.

items.title: YC's batch data: hard tech 8% to 20%, median batch-exit revenue up from US$8k to US$20k/month
items.why: Skim for the numbers, which are proprietary and quantified; skip the discussion around them, which is anecdotal. Thirty-six minutes for what is really four statistics.
key_points: Hard tech has gone from 8% to 20% of the batch over the last 12-18 months.
Median accepted company is pre-revenue and pre-product. Median revenue at batch end has gone from c.US$8k/month to c.US$20k/month (+ve on velocity, off a tiny base).
Category detail: robotics 1% to 6-7%, industrial manufacturing 4% to 10%, defence c.1.5% to c.5%, plus two other categories moving from c.1% to c.3-4%.

Drivers offered: SpaceX's IPO creating a cohort wanting to build in space; war salience pushing founders toward defence and US reshoring; and AI collapsing the software component that used to make hard tech hard.
Observation on founder age — a resurgence of experienced founders in their late thirties to fifties, attributed to hard tech needing research backgrounds.
items.read_across: A 20% hard-tech batch at YC is an early read on where private capital formation is heading in defence, industrial reshoring and space.

items.title: Odd Lots on pass-throughs and S-corps: where the tax cuts actually went, and how many wealthy Americans there really are
items.why: Skim. Structurally useful on a part of the US tax base that rarely gets covered properly, and the source is a Treasury-commissioned pass through IRS microdata. Sixty minutes is long for the payload, but the framing is not available elsewhere.
key_points: Thesis: when tax breaks for the wealthy are discussed the frame is usually a Bezos effective-rate story, but the material cuts since the 1980s and again under the current administration have run through S-corps and pass-through entities.
These get framed politically as small business; the book's finding is that many are very large and very wealthy.

Provenance matters: the work started as a Treasury Department commission to sift IRS data to establish who these owners are and how many there are — the department had not been able to do it because the datasets were not linked.
Reframes the inequality discussion away from a 1%/0.1% concentration story toward a much broader base of business-owning wealth.
items.read_across: Relevant to US consumption and private-wealth AUM assumptions: the affluent cohort is wider and more business-income-dependent than a top-0.1% frame implies.

items.title: UBS's Lovell: earnings not the Fed drive the tape; multiple already compressed 22x to 19x
items.why: Skim — twenty-one minutes and the numbers are specific. It is the bull case against this week's hike, which is worth holding next to the Journal episode rather than instead of it.
key_points: The call: 'earnings not the Fed are driving this market. Another rate hike would be a speed bump, not a stop sign' — buy the pullbacks.
Most recent season approached 30% EPS growth. Forecasts c.25% EPS growth this year and 14% next, both above longer-term trend (+ve).
Valuation has already absorbed a lot: the multiple has come in from 22x at the start of the year to 19x now, so higher rates and bond yields are partly priced.
Concedes equity markets historically struggle at the start of a hiking cycle and expects near-term volatility, but argues any pullback is shallow. Looking for c.10% upside rather than 20%.
Points to broadening earnings growth as evidence of a healthier bull market, and argues a predictable, methodical 25bp cadence is what the market needs.
Flags pressure specifically on long-duration and housing-sensitive areas (-ve).
items.read_across: 19x with 14% forward EPS is the bull's arithmetic. The stated vulnerability — long duration and housing-sensitive — is where to look if the hike cadence turns out to be less methodical than assumed.

items.title: Bostrom on the week AI safety went mainstream
items.why: Skim, and prefer this one over the Hard Fork episode on the same story — Bostrom is the primary intellectual source and this is 66 minutes against Hard Fork's 84 for largely the same events. Note the first three minutes are cross-promo ads.
key_points: The week's chain of events, as set out: Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher, posted that employees at both believe AI could 'kill us all by the end of the decade'; the post went viral; other researchers came forward with the same concern.
Then Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay calling for the industry to slow model development, and Sam Altman said he agreed — and added that OpenAI will not go public this year.
Bostrom is positioned as the longest-standing student of the problem; Superintelligence (2014) shaped how Musk, Altman and Sutskever framed it.

He characterises the moment as confusing and perplexing, and says the view that there are significant risks including existential ones is quite widespread among people close to the technology and inside the frontier labs.
items.read_across: 'OpenAI will not go public this year' is the only directly market-relevant item in the chain, and it came attached to a safety argument rather than a market one.

items.title: Inception's Ermon on diffusion for text: parallel token output as the inference-cost attack
items.why: Skim. A credible technical challenger thesis from one of the originators of diffusion, aimed squarely at inference cost. The evidence offered is still sub-billion-parameter and academic, so treat it as a thesis to monitor rather than a demonstrated result.
key_points: Ermon is a Stanford professor and one of the originators of diffusion; score-based generative models date to his group's 2019 work.

The claim: a transformer trained as a diffusion model on the same data was significantly faster, because diffusion outputs many tokens simultaneously rather than autoregressively (+ve for latency and cost per token).
Scale caveat stated plainly — the comparison was at under a billion parameters and fairly academic.
Supporting argument from adjacent markets: diffusion already dominates short-form generated video, which is a large enough use case that hardware is being built for it.
Company positioning is speed and efficiency as the competitive axis over the next few years, explicitly against the large labs.
items.read_across: If parallel decoding generalises to large models it compresses inference cost per token, which cuts against the inference-demand read from the Brown episode. Worth holding both.

items.title: Gurley on institutional failure: Surfside and the 737 MAX as templates for how bad news gets suppressed
items.why: Skim. Not an AI or markets talk despite the venue — it is an argument about why institutions fail to act on information they already have, built on two forensic case studies. Useful as a diligence frame; no direct positioning content.
key_points: Case one, Champlain Towers South, Surfside, June 2021, 98 dead. Three institutional failures — design flaws from the outset, poor maintenance scheduling, and a condo board that did not act on an inspection report — sitting on top of a technical one (saltwater corrosion of the pool deck collapsing into the basement and taking out structural columns).
His emphasis is on who produced the knowledge: NYT investigative work, plus four parallel investigations including NIST, a Florida grand jury, and 17 victim suits consolidated into one class.
Case two, the 737 MAX. Root cause was that the engine was too large and had to be moved forward on the wing; two crashes followed, October 2018 and March 2019.
The suppression point: roughly 45 days after the first crash almost everyone knew MCAS was at fault. Ted Cruz accused the head of the FAA of being a captured regulator in Senate testimony.
Credits sustained specialist coverage — Dominic Gates had covered Boeing for the Seattle Times for 16 years.
items.read_across: The transferable point for diligence: the gap between when a defect is known internally and when it is priced is an institutional-incentive question, not an information-availability one.

items.title: Hard Fork on the AI safety week — and the show's final episode
items.why: Skim only if you want the media-side colour. The substance overlaps the Prof G Bostrom episode almost entirely — same Coxon post, same Dario essay — and at 84 minutes with an exit AMA attached it is the longer, thinner version of the two. Take Bostrom instead.
key_points: Same triggering chain as the Bostrom episode: Coxon's viral resignation post saying neither OpenAI nor Anthropic is acting responsibly.
The hosts' own read on why it landed this time — the response to the OpenAI/Hugging Face incident had already shifted how people receive the message, where a few weeks earlier it would not have.
One host notes candidly that the post did not faze him, and takes that as evidence he is in a bubble.
Disclosure carried on air: the NYT is suing OpenAI, Microsoft and Perplexity.
This is the show's final episode, with an exit AMA occupying a large share of the runtime.

items.title: a16z's Elman on what makes a consumer AI product stick
items.why: Skim if you underwrite consumer software; otherwise skip. The framework is sound but familiar — do one thing well, become a habit, then earn the right to expand. Sixty minutes for one reusable datapoint and one structural argument.
key_points: The datapoint: ChatGPT cited at 900m weekly active users.

The stickiness test he applies: a product has to be good enough out of the box that the user either stops doing something else or hands more behaviours over to it — attention is cheap, displacement is not.
Sequencing argument: start by doing one thing exceptionally well, become a habit, then expand. Products that start broad do not get there.
Forward view is that trust becomes the binding constraint as agents move into shopping, entertainment and acting on a user's behalf with known preferences.

items.title: Isaacman's NASA address: a programme critique delivered as a keynote, with no investable specifics
items.why: Skip. The NASA administrator criticising legacy programme structure is genuinely newsworthy, but the 39 minutes carry no budget numbers, no contract decisions and no timelines — it is a keynote. If you hold space or defence exposure, the two specifics below are the whole extractable payload.
key_points: His criticism of SLS/Orion: the vehicle is less efficient than Saturn V at converting launch mass into payload headed for the moon, and there is more time between Artemis 1 and Artemis 2 than spanned all 12 Gemini missions flown 60 years earlier (-ve for legacy programme credibility).
Stated priority for the next capability step is nuclear power and propulsion; he notes billions were spent on nuclear programmes that have not left the laboratory since 1965.
Framing is explicitly great-power competition — China operating 25,000 miles of high-speed rail and a few years from its own Apollo 11 moment.
Concedes the change is externally driven: absent this president and the geopolitical competition, he suspects very little would have changed.

items.title: Goldman's Sykes on bringing the Olympics to LA: scale figures, but the funding question is not answered
items.why: Skip. Recorded live at a conference, and it stays at the level of scale statistics and personal history. The one question with investment content — the LA28 funding mix — is raised and not resolved.
key_points: Sykes is co-head of Global M&A at Goldman and president of the US Olympic Committee; he led the original LA bid for 2024.
Scale: 17,000 athletes across the Olympic and Paralympic Games, and 15m tickets to be sold in Los Angeles — against 104 matches for the World Cup across Mexico and the US.
The funding mix for the 2028 LA games is asked about directly and not answered with figures.

items.title: Bloomberg Money: household finance segments, and a KKR regime-change essay that is mentioned but not discussed
items.why: Skip. Forty-four minutes of personal-finance television — cost of raising children, student loan rates, college sports going professional. KKR's Henry McVey is introduced around a regime-change essay on global macro and asset allocation, which would have been the reason to listen, and the segment does not get to it. The same show's 18 September episode is the shorter one with actual market content.
key_points: Henry McVey, KKR partner and head of global macro and asset allocation, is introduced around a 'really important regime change essay' — the essay itself is not worked through.
Household figures cited: cost of raising a child put at US$300,000 excluding college; graduate programme costs of US$125,000 per year over two to three years at 9% loan rates.
Segment thesis is the 'Bank of Mom and Dad' — grandparents and parents stepping in because families need more capital to raise children.
Also covers the DOJ targeting a broader set of colleges, and 23-hour equity trading, on which the host is openly sceptical.

items.title: In Good Company Friday wrap-up: a process-simplification framework, no market content
items.why: Skip. Fourteen minutes of the hosts recapping their own week's guest on process simplification. The one line worth having is below; there is nothing on NBIM's positioning, which is the reason to listen to this show.
key_points: The framework discussed is John McNeill's Algorithm — question every requirement, delete every unnecessary step, simplify, accelerate, then automate last.
The transferable line: automating or adding AI on top of an unsimplified process is 'like pouring cement on top of a process'.
Applied to the fund, they concede compliance and governance steps cannot be removed, but are changing reporting frequency and asset revaluation cadence.

items.title: The Journal on prenups: off-mandate
items.why: Skip. Twenty-one minutes on prenuptial agreements as a middle-class financial planning tool. No market, allocation or product content. The one statistic is below if you want it for a wealth-management conversation.
key_points: A 2023 survey put one in five married or engaged adults as having a prenup, skewed to Gen Z and millennials.
Framing has shifted from a stigmatised contract toward a financial planning tool, attributed partly to TikTok and Instagram circulation.

gaps: AI Ascent remains unobtainable — Spotify-exclusive, absent from Apple and public RSS. Paid transcript vendors do not solve it, since they also index audio from public RSS.
Sharp Tech shipped a Preview only, discarded as a derivative episode; Exponent has not published since 2022 and should probably come off the list.
BofA's 'Signals & Noise' came back as a partial transcript, so the structured-income figures beyond the headline sizing are indicative rather than confirmed.
Thin day on the subscribed list — 4 episodes against 14 from the watchlist. Capital Allocators, Invest Like the Best and Acquired did not publish in the window.
